text: From this follows a further praise, and Johnson states it with his usual plainness: "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men" (Johnson 1765). Other dramatists, as he saw them, raised their persons above the common level, giving them sentiments no living man would utter and a manner of speech fitted rather to admiration than to belief. Johnson counts Shakespeare's abstention from this practice among his chief merits. The persons of the plays speak as the reader himself would have spoken had he stood in the same place and felt the same pressure; their words are drawn from ordinary life, and they move us because we recognise them. Nor does this hold only where the action is probable. When a ghost walks the platform or witches meet upon the heath, the event lies outside experience, yet the speech of those who witness it remains within it. The marvel belongs to the plot; the dialogue stays level with life, so that Hamlet questions the spirit of his father as any son might question a thing so dreadful, and Macbeth broods upon the prophecy as an ambitious man would brood upon a promise of a crown.
